evidence.label: An infinite finitely presented simple amenable group

headline: One infinite group that is simple, amenable and described by finitely many rules at once.
scope: Existence of one infinite, finitely presented, simple, amenable group. Lean covers the existence; the paper's later general claims across families are not included.
plain: Three traits of infinite groups matter here. Finitely many rules describe them, they cannot be broken into smaller pieces, and they allow fair averages. Groups with the last two traits were known since 2013, but none with all three. This paper proves such a group exists, with a Lean formalization listed. The group moves pieces of polygons around inside a finite set of squares.
doesNot: This does not bound the number of generators or rules, and Lean does not cover the general claims about central kernels and enlargements.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Kate Juschenko and Nicolas Monod, whose work gave infinite finitely generated simple amenable groups
scorecard.significanceWhy: Whether a finitely presented infinite simple amenable group exists was a recorded open question in group theory.

explanation:
Take the integers and the window D = {1, 2, …, 100}. Shift the window by 1. You get {2, …, 101}. The old and new windows differ in only two numbers: 1 and 101. So the change is 2 out of 100, or 2%. A longer window makes the share smaller. This is the Følner condition: for any finite set of moves and any ε > 0, some finite set D barely changes under each move. Groups with this property are called amenable. They allow fair averages.

A group is simple when its only normal subgroups are the trivial group and the whole group[1]. A normal subgroup is one that conjugation by any element leaves unchanged. It is finitely presented when finitely many generators and rules describe it[1]. The question asked whether an infinite group can have all three properties together[2].

Partial answers were known. Juschenko and Monod proved in 2013 that full groups of minimal Cantor systems are amenable[14]. With earlier work of Matui, this gave infinite finitely generated simple amenable groups[3]. Finite presentation was the property left out[4]. Matui showed the groups from minimal subshifts are not finitely presented[5]. There is a deeper reason. Those groups embed locally into finite groups, so a finitely presented one would be residually finite[6]. Residually finite means every nonidentity element survives in some finite image. An infinite simple group cannot be residually finite[6]. Any nontrivial map to a finite group would have to be injective, which is impossible for an infinite group.

The paper proves there is an infinite finitely presented simple amenable group[7]. The group is an alternating subgroup of a polygon exchange group on finitely many squares[8]. A polygon exchange cuts squares into polygons and slides the pieces by translations. The polygon edges lie on lines in four directions[9]. Their levels use the golden ratio τ = (1 + √5)/2 ≈ 1.618. The obstacle was amenability in two dimensions. Elek and Monod built a two-dimensional Cantor system whose full group contains a free group, which is not amenable[10]. Here, random polygon partitions that move almost unchanged under each generator give the averages[11]. A homology argument and a relation-propagation step give finite presentation.

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has a formal proof that there is one group that is infinite, finitely presented, simple and amenable. It does not include the paper's later general claims. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if it holds, and the existence theorem has a Lean formalization. The general claims across families are not in the Lean note. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A group with finite sets that barely change under each move; equivalently, it allows fair averages.
For every finite set of moves and every ε, some finite set changes by less than an ε share under each move.
A nontrivial group whose only normal subgroups are the trivial group and itself.
Described by finitely many generators and finitely many defining rules.
Every nonidentity element stays nonidentity in some finite image of the group.
A continuous map acting on a Cantor set, a totally disconnected space like the infinite binary sequences.
A group of maps that cut regions into polygons and move each piece by a translation.
